title: Waveland, MS | CRS Activity 510
text:
CRS Planning Support
This project was completed using funding allocated by the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to support coastal communities in pursuing Community Rating System (CRS) credit.
I contributed to the development of the City of Waveland’s Community Rating System (CRS) Activity 510 floodplain management plans, supporting the technical analysis, mapping, and plan development.
My work included conducting flood risk and vulnerability analyses, developing maps and other GIS-based analyses, compiling and interpreting flood insurance and claims statistics, and contributing extensively to plan writing. These analyses helped characterize local flood hazards, identify vulnerable properties and areas, and inform floodplain management priorities and mitigation strategies.
Datasets used in this project include:

County tax assessor data
NOAA sea level rise extent
NOAA sea level depths
SLOSH
OpenFEMA NFIP policies and claims
HUC watersheds

I also supported the City’s CRS planning efforts by developing a property-level database for substantial damage management planning, providing communities with an organized framework for identifying and tracking properties following flood events. For repetitive loss planning, I conducted repetitive loss area analyses to identify and characterize concentrations of repetitive flood losses and support the development of targeted mitigation actions.

title: Climate Change & Federal Aid Dispersements
text:
Climate Change & Post-Harvey Federal Aid
In this project, I conducted a spatial analysis examining the relationship between climate change attributable flood damages and federal disaster assistance at the census tract level. The study area was Harris County, TX following Hurricane Harvey (2017).
I integrated modeled flood damages with census tract-level National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) and FEMA Individual Assistance (IA) disbursement data. Using climate attribution estimates from peer-reviewed research, the analysis compared damages under scenarios in which climate change increased Harvey’s rainfall by 20% and 38%. I applied spatial lag regression models to estimate both direct and spatial spillover relationships between attributable damages and federal recovery expenditures.
The results showed that while both attributable and non-attributable flood damages were associated with federal aid, climate change attributable damages generally had larger effect sizes, particularly for Individual Assistance.
The research highlights an important fiscal dimension of climate change: as climate change intensifies disaster damages, it can also increase the financial burden of recovery borne by federal programs and insurers.

title: EPA Brownfield Assessment
text:
EPA Brownfield Coalition Assessment
I contributed to a successful $1.5 million FY2026 EPA Brownfields grant application by compiling and analyzing social vulnerability and community demographic data, developing maps to communicate conditions in priority areas, and contributing to the written grant narrative. This work helped document community needs and provide a data-driven foundation for the proposed brownfields activities.
I also support the administration and reporting of previously awarded Brownfields grants (FY2019 and FY2023), including compiling information on project activities and outcomes. In addition, I am helping develop a public-facing website highlighting Brownfields accomplishments and success stories, translating project results into accessible information that communicates the program’s community impact.

About Me





Photo taken at a Community Resilience Center Retreat in Corpus Christi, TX (2026)





Photo taken in Hattiesburg, MS during an EPA Brownfield Site Assessment “tank yank.”




As a Coastal Mississippi Resilience Fellow, I analyze, visualize, and communicate a wide variety of data types, including demographic, land use, hazard, and insurance-related datasets, to support planning and decision making. I have supported municipal planning, community engagement, project implementation, and have helped secure over $6 million in state, regional, and federal grant funds for communities across southern Mississippi.
Before my fellowship, I worked as a research assistant on an NSF funded project, where I integrated structure-level datasets created by scientists with the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and The Water Institute into a comprehensive hierarchical geospatial dataset covering nearly 1 million structures in southern Louisiana.
In August 2026, I graduated with my Ph.D. in sociology, where my research focused on inequities in flooding and disaster recovery, particularly for flood impacts that are attributable to climate change. Before this, I graduated with a M.S. from the University of North Texas in 2022 and B.S. from Texas A&M University in 2020.

title: D’Iberville, MS | CRS Activity 610
text:
CRS Planning Support
This project was completed using funding allocated by the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to support coastal communities in pursuing Community Rating System (CRS) credit.
From October 2025 to present (August 2026), I have supported resilience planners in the development of Community Rating System (CRS) Activity 610 flood response plans, contributing to both the planning process and the technical analysis required to support CRS crediting.
My work included participating in stakeholder meetings, contributing to plan writing, and compiling and analyzing flood-risk and community data. I also supported communities in selecting appropriate coastal and riverine flood scenarios, using SLOSH storm surge modeling and NOAA riverine flood inundation data to evaluate potential flood conditions and inform response planning.
A major component of my work involved spatial analysis of buildings covered by each flood response plan, identifying structures within the selected flood scenarios and supporting the calculation of CRS credit adjustments. I developed maps and other GIS-based analyses to communicate flood extent, document plan coverage, and support the planning and CRS documentation process.

title: EEIA & Post-Harvey NFIP Insurance Participation
text:
Climate Change & Post-Harvey NFIP Policy Participation
Using census tract level estimates of Hurricane Harvey’s flood impacts, I investigated whether neighborhoods experiencing a greater proportion of flooding attributable to climate change subsequently showed different patterns of NFIP policy uptake, renewals, and cancellations.
The analysis combined climate impact attribution data with NFIP policy information and tract-level socioeconomic and housing characteristics. Using spatial statistical models, I analyzed whether greater exposure to climate change-attributable flooding was associated with changes in post-Harvey flood insurance uptake and how these relationships varied across communities.
The analysis provided evidence that climate-attributable flooding was associated with distinct post-disaster NFIP participation outcomes—and that these outcomes diverged by neighborhood income.
